sources.title: Nyala
sources.note: 2025 regional assessment: Least Concern; regional trend stable.

size.note: Wikipedia gives head-and-body length as 135–195 cm. Males stand over one metre at the shoulder (Animal Diversity Web) and up to about 110 cm if that 'over one metre' is taken with the commonly cited male height; females are up to 90 cm (Wikipedia) or slightly less than a metre (ADW). The overall shoulder-height bounds used here are 90–110 cm, with this caveat. Mass follows Wikipedia and ADW: males 98–125 kg, females 55–68 kg. Male horns are 60–83 cm (Wikipedia) or up to 80 cm (ADW), with one or two twists and yellow tips. A calf weighs about 5 kg.

summary: A mid-sized, spiral-horned antelope of riverine thicket, with the strongest sexual dimorphism of its group. Males are dark and shaggy, with a dorsal crest, yellow lower legs and horns; females and young are bright rufous with many close white stripes. In Kruger it is a resident of southern and far-northern riverine bush.
description: Sexual dimorphism is marked. Adult males are dark brown to slate-grey, often with a bluish tinge; the coat is shaggy, with a white dorsal crest, a throat fringe, and yellow-tawny lower legs. Body stripes are faint or absent in older males. Only males have horns, 60–83 cm, with one or two twists and yellow tips. Females and juveniles are rusty or rufous brown, with ten or more clear white vertical stripes and other white marks on the face, throat, flanks and thighs; they are hornless. Both sexes have a white chevron between the eyes. It should not be confused with the mountain nyala of Ethiopia.
habits: A shy, mainly browsing antelope of dense thicket. It may feed by day in warm, dry weather and more by night in the rainy season, and prefers waterholes to open ground. It is not territorial; ranges can overlap. Animals live in small single-sex or mixed groups of up to about ten, though old males are often alone. In Kruger it is associated with riverine thicket in the south and the far north (Pafuri and Punda Maria), rather than with open grassland.

diet.summary: A herbivore that browses foliage and also takes fruits and grasses, and needs fresh water.

young: A single calf, weighing about 5 kg, is born after a gestation of seven months, usually in cover such as a thicket. The calf is hidden for up to 18 days and is nursed at intervals. It stays with the mother until the next calf is born, when males in rut may drive it away. Exact calving months for Kruger were not found.

predators.note: Not a mammal in this guide; listed because it is a documented predator of this species.

habitat: Thickets in dense or dry savanna woodland, especially riverine cover. In Kruger, one source places it in the riverine thickets of the south and the far north, including the Luvuvhu and Limpopo in the Pafuri area.

similar.note: Kudu is taller and narrower. A kudu bull has much longer horns with two and a half open spirals and no yellow lower legs; a kudu cow is greyer or browner, not bright rufous, and has fewer, more widely spaced stripes than a female nyala.
Bushbuck is smaller. The female bushbuck is less brightly rufous, and the male lacks the nyala bull's long shaggy crest and yellow lower legs.

population.notes: One source describes nyala in the southern and far-northern riverine thickets of Kruger but does not give a recent park count. An earlier figure of about 3,000 animals in the greater Kruger area (Anderson 2013) is cited on the EWT Nyala page, and is kept here as a previous estimate. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf Regional Red List status is Least Concern, with a stable national trend.

previousEstimates.notes: Greater Kruger, about 3,000 animals, cited on the EWT Nyala page (Anderson 2013). A single published number is stored as both bounds. This is not a Kruger-only census and is not used as the current estimate.
